How to create photo 3D online

Upload a source image, generate a 3D draft, inspect geometry and textures, then export the GLB when the result is ready.

Upload an Image

2

Review the 3D Pass

Download Outputs

photo3d.org FAQ

Fast answers about local 3D tools, browser previews, file preparation, accounts, rights, and support.

1
What can I generate on photo3d.org?

photo3d.org turns one photo into a textured 3D model you can download as GLB. You choose from 40+ model lanes, including Trellis, Hunyuan 3D, Tripo3D, Rodin, and Meshy, and the workspace queues the job against your account.

2
Do I need an account?

No for local Free Tools and browser previews. Sign in only when you want saved generation history, account credits, or managed AI 3D tasks.

3
Which tool should I open first?

If you already have a photo, start with the generator at the top of this page. The Free Tools are best used afterwards to check scale, textures, and file format before you hand the model on.

4
Are the browser tools local?

Yes. The 50+ viewer, editor, inspector, conversion, texture, scale, compression, and image tools run inside your browser, never upload your files to a server, and never spend generation credits.

5
What should I check before upload or handoff?

Center the object, use a plain background, and keep the whole silhouette in frame. photo3d.org reads GLB, glTF, OBJ, STL, PLY, FBX, 3MF, PNG, JPG, and WebP, so you can verify texture memory and real-world scale before paying for a run.

6
Can I use generated 3D assets commercially?

It depends on which model lane produced the file, the provider terms behind that lane, and what rights you hold in the source photo. photo3d.org does not claim ownership of your uploads, but check those terms before shipping a GLB in a product, game, ad, or client deliverable.

7
How do I contact support?

Email support@photo3d.org with your account address and the task ID from your activity list. Failed photo 3D runs are reviewed for a credit refund under the Refund Policy.

STL, GLB and OBJ from one photo: 5 free models a day, the colours on the side you photographed.

What you get

One clear object, fully in frame, photographed from a slight angle so some depth is visible: a figurine, a mug, a shoe, a toy, a vase, a piece of furniture. We cut the object out of the background first, so a plain background helps but is not required.

People, animals and very thin or see-through things (glass, wire, hair) are the hardest. Groups of objects come out as one lump. A photo with several people, or with glasses, often gives a distorted face or glasses that sit too low, so use one person per photo, facing the camera.

From a single photo the AI has to guess the back of the object. For simple and symmetric things that guess is usually good; for anything with a detailed back, expect it to be plausible rather than exact.Edit Photos

Objects whose detail is mostly flat artwork, lettering or fine relief (badges, coins, logos) come out as a rough shape.

Printing it
How long it takes, and the limits
How to turn a photo into a 3D model

A solid  3D shape of the object in your photo, which you can rotate right here on the page before you download it. The STL and OBJ files are sized so the longest side is 100 mm and the model stands on its base, ready to scale in your slicer.

The GLB and OBJ carry the colours of your photo, painted onto the shape. The back, which your camera never saw, gets colours estimated from the front, so it is less exact. The STL is the shape only: which is exactly what a  3D printer uses. Fine surface detail such as small text, engraving or filigree is shown by the photo colours in the preview, not built into the shape, so it can look rough or be missing in a slicer. One subject per image

The 3D reconstruction focuses on the dominant object in the frame. If the image contains multiple objects or a busy scene, the model will try to reconstruct everything as a single surface, which produces a confusing, low-quality mesh. Use Image to Image to isolate a single subject from a complex scene before converting.

Square or near-square crops work best

The 3D model works best with square or near-square images. If your subject is a very wide or very tall crop, the model may distort the proportions slightly. Use the free Image Converter or Image to Image to reframe to 1:1 before uploading for the most accurate geometry.

Even, diffuse lighting over harsh directional light

Strong shadows bake into the texture and can confuse the depth estimation. A softbox, overcast outdoor light or a light tent for products will produce geometry that matches the object's real shape rather than the shadow pattern.

Sharp focus on the full subject

Shallow depth-of-field (bokeh) blurs parts of the subject, and the model has no way to know the actual shape of a blurred region. Use a narrower aperture so the entire object is in sharp focus from front to back.

Higher resolution inputs produce denser meshes

Upload the highest-resolution version of the image you have. The model downscales internally as needed, but starting with more pixels means finer surface detail and a more accurate texture bake in the output .glb file. Run your image through the Image Upscaler at 2× or 4× before converting if you are starting from a low-resolution source.

Solid, opaque objects over transparent or reflective ones

Glass, mirrors, highly polished chrome and transparent materials are notoriously hard for single-view reconstruction - The model cannot see "through" or correctly interpret the reflection. Matte, opaque surfaces reconstruct with significantly more fidelity. If your subject is reflective, try using Image to Image to repaint it with a matte finish before converting.

Use AI-generated images as the input

Our AI Image Generator produces clean, well-lit images on plain backgrounds by default - Making them nearly perfect inputs for 3D conversion. Generate a product or character image first, then convert it to 3D in a single workflow entirely on img.now.
